svg.aria-label: Traffic flow: an app pod’s wg-client sidecar sends its internet-bound traffic through a WireGuard tunnel on UDP 51820, via a ClusterIP Service, to the WireGuard server pod, whose agent forwards it from wg0 to gluetun’s tun0 and out through a commercial VPN provider to the internet — while cluster DNS, pods, Services and nodes (the Wireguard’s localCIDRs) stay local and never enter the tunnel, and a blackhole route, gluetun’s killswitch and the client’s missing eth0 default route drop traffic rather than leak it when the tunnel is down; the sidecar, gluetun and the egress path are designed but not yet implemented.
svg.text: Out Through the Tunnel: How a Pod’s Traffic Leaves the Cluster
Internet-bound traffic rides WireGuard to an in-cluster server and exits through a VPN provider; cluster traffic never enters the tunnel.

text.tspan: • The sidecar mints its own key; the
private half never leaves the pod.
• It points the default route at wg0; app
containers start once the tunnel is up.
• Cluster ranges keep their usual route,
server pod; a pod that is not
• The agent ends every client’s tunnel on wg0 and
• gluetun holds the VPN connection on tun0, with its
• Provider credentials come from a Secret.
• The Wireguard’s localCIDRs list the pod, Service and node ranges; the sidecar routes them
• DNS is untouched: in-cluster names resolve as before, and the server’s ClusterIP is local too.

svg.text: Fails Closed When the Tunnel Is Down

text.tspan: • With tun0 or gluetun down, client traffic is dropped, never sent out the node’s own address.
• Server: anything from wg0 that tun0 cannot take hits a blackhole route.
• Client: wg0 is the only default route, so no tunnel means no route out.
